title: Position Sizing When Markets Break feat. Rob Carver - Systematic Investor - Ep.386

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Position Sizing When Markets Break feat. Rob Carver - Systematic Investor - Ep.386.docx

speakers: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
summary: Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor Ep.386 (Feb 2026): Rob Carver and Niels on the silver crash of 30 Jan 2026 (volatility-adjusted sizing, liquidity, Hunt 1979), a new Fed chair, trend update, listener questions on correlation/covariance estimation for vol targeting, a Man AHL paper on traditional vs alternative markets in trend portfolios, and an FT article on quant/AI convergence. Conclusions: vol-adjusted sizing and diversification protect in parabolic reversals; crisis-alpha seekers should favour traditional liquid futures.

coverage.note: nothing actionable: intro, small talk and a paper title about total portfolio approach
Silver Freaky Friday setup; CTA positions as function of trend and volatility; dynamic optimisation; vol-adjustment variants
Rob silver trades, buy/sell dates and prices; effect of vol adjustment vs non-adjusting CTAs
Stop losses and volatility; liquidity differences across metals
Liquidity disappears in crisis, crowded vol-adjusting strategies, position sizing and diversification as risk management
CTAs as buffer rather than cause; Hunt silver 1979 and margin hikes; systematic risk management
Silver supply structure; cross-market dislocations incl. natural gas; commodities in trend universe; new Fed chair introduction
Tariff tantrum behavioural mistake; Fed chair uncertainty and muted bond reaction
Silver sell-off positioning; systematic vs discretionary; Google capex bubble comment
Trend barometer 64, Feb breadth, Bitcoin shorts, index data; listener question starts
Pedro question: correlation scaling for vol target; 0.7 origin; estimation window
Estimating correlation vs vol separately, predictability R-squared, vol targeting removes need for vol estimate
Man AHL paper: three market categories
Factor vs idiosyncratic return decomposition; unconstrained optimisation 30% traditional
Standalone vs 60/40 add-on; crisis-conditional optimisation favours traditional markets
Cash efficiency and margin constraints; 2008 cash machine; summary of choice
Investor fit; FT Alphaville quant-AI convergence, machine learning in systematic finance
AI use in funds, execution research, talent pay

completeness_estimate: 0.84 - first reader captured the silver crash mechanics, sizing and paper findings well; missed side mechanisms (binary versus continuous sizing, daily-rebalance gap, stop-loss gap risk, liquidity filter, Fed chair institutional points, TACO behaviour, correlation-turnover point)

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: positions that are function of two things. The strength of the trend and the volatility of the instrument you're trading.
claims.claim: A CTA's position in an instrument is a function of trend strength (forecast) and the instrument's volatility, so rising volatility can reduce exposure even while the trend signal strengthens.
claims.direction: position down when volatility rises, up when forecast rises
claims.conditions: applies to continuous-forecast, vol-scaled CTAs
claims.testable: yes: position = forecast / volatility is a testable rule

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: I basically dynamically optimize my portfolio every day to match to get the best possible match I could do to a sort of abstract portfolio
claims.claim: A small account trades a dynamically optimised subset of 250 futures, matching an idealised large portfolio, so it may hold no position in an instrument despite a strong forecast.
claims.conditions: small portfolio constraints

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um and also of course, some CTAs take volatility into account when they initially buy a position, but they don't make any further adjustments to that position as volatility changes.
claims.claim: CTAs differ: some adjust position continuously for volatility changes, some size on volatility only at entry, which drives very different outcomes in parabolic moves.
claims.testable: yes: compare continuous vs entry-only vol scaling

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: on the 31st of December, I sold a contract and that would have been inevitably because the volatility increased
claims.claim: Rob bought silver in late Nov/early Dec as the forecast grew, then sold contracts on 31 Dec and the following Monday because volatility rose, so the position shrank into the crash while the trend signal stayed long.
claims.conditions: during parabolic rises

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: even a day like Friday where silver dropped by the most in one day since
claims.claim: Silver fell by the most in one day in 45 to 47 years on 30 Jan 2026, but a normal-speed trend system's signal stays long after one negative day.
claims.conditions: unless the trend system is very fast
claims.testable: yes: trend persistence after one-day extremes

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: So I bought I bought into my silver position um at levels of 53 and 59 dollars per ounce respectively.
claims.claim: Rob's silver trades (bought at $53 and $59, sold at $71 and $81) were profitable even though the price peaked at $110-120 before the crash, because the crash returned silver to levels of weeks earlier.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: because what they would have done is seen the value of the silver in their portfolio kind of get bigger and bigger and bigger.
claims.claim: Without continuous vol adjustment, silver grew as a share of the portfolio during the run-up, so the one-day drop caused a very large loss for such CTAs.
claims.conditions: non-vol-adjusting, highly levered CTAs

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: think about being up 72% on the Thursday and ending the month up 27%.
claims.claim: One highly levered CTA without vol adjustment went from +72% to +27% on the month in one day on Freaky Friday.
claims.conditions: high leverage, no vol scaling

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: if you do increase your stop with you also should reduce your position at the same time
claims.claim: If a volatility-based stop is raised as volatility rises, position size should be reduced simultaneously, otherwise risk increases.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um if you don't increase your stop level as volatility rises, then you you you risk basically being shaken out the position too early.
claims.claim: A stop that does not widen with volatility risks being shaken out of a trend too early.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: people treat liquidity as a constant number as a constant number of volume of contracts they can expect to trade, but of course it isn't, right?
claims.claim: Liquidity is not constant: after a run-up and a pullback the buyers are gone, so liquidity vanishes in crises, and more so in less-liquid markets.
claims.conditions: less liquid markets, momentum-chasing entrants

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: what you really need to do is go back a year or 2 years and say, "Well, over a longer period of time, what does liquidity look like?"
claims.claim: Judge liquidity over a one to two year history, not recent volume/open-interest spikes caused by tourists.
claims.indicator: volume and open interest over 1-2 years
claims.conditions: hot markets with recent volume spikes

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um so anyone who sells on the hint of volatility spiking, the the more people there are in a particular market like that, the more it'll magnify the move.
claims.claim: CTAs, risk parity and other quant strategies all cut exposure when vol spikes, so crowding amplifies volatility-driven sell-offs.
claims.conditions: when many funds vol-adjust the same market
claims.testable: partly: amplification is hard to isolate

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um and the two key things about risk management are position sizing um and diversification.
claims.claim: Position sizing by volatility and diversification limited Rob's loss to 3% of account on the silver crash day, versus much larger for concentrated or unscaled funds.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um so on Friday, I lost 3% of my total account value because I have a reasonably diversified portfolio.
claims.claim: A 3% one-day loss was in line with other CTAs at similar annual vol.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker. The comment that a 3% one-day loss was in line with other CTAs at similar annual volatility is Niels's, based on what he saw from managers he follows; Rob only reported his own 3% loss.
correction.fix: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen: a 3% loss on the crash day was very decent for a trend manager at that annual volatility, matching what he saw from the managers he can follow.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: the majority of the larger CTAs, they're they're the ones who've been selling silver all the way through January, as you rightly said
claims.claim: Larger CTAs were reducing silver notional as volatility expanded, so they dampen rather than cause parabolic moves.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: he kept buying now for borrowed money. So, the leverage of his position became, you know, quite high.
claims.claim: Hunt brothers silver 1979: leveraged buying with borrowed money, exchange margin hikes and a rise from $6 to $50 ended in catastrophe; pyramiding and leverage repeat across eras.
claims.conditions: parabolic markets with leverage and rising margins

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: So, COMEX started to change the rules on margins.
claims.claim: Exchanges raise margins in parabolic moves, forcing leveraged holders to liquidate (seen in 1979 and again in Jan 2026).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: We manage our risk in a systematic, dispassionate way.
claims.claim: Managers with decades of experience avoid emotional attachment and manage risk systematically.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: It's only like 30% of the production actually every year is specifically mined as silver. The rest comes from a byproduct of gold and copper.
claims.claim: Only about 30% of silver supply is mined as silver, so supply is less controllable and the market more volatile than gold.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: long short quant equity factors have gone a balmy
claims.claim: The 30 Jan week saw dislocations across markets: quant equity factors, Bitcoin and AI stocks, while Rob's trend portfolio coped.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: from the 9th of January to the 30th of January, it um was up something like 60%. And then on the 2nd of February, in 1 day, it lost 26%.
claims.claim: March natural gas gained 60% then lost 26% in a day on weather, showing large reversals outside precious metals.
claims.conditions: weather events

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: people need to realize how important it is to have the commodities as part of their trend following universe because this is where we sometimes see lots and lots of opportunities
claims.claim: Commodities in a trend universe provide opportunities often independent of equity risk-off events.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: did something very silly and non systematic and sold all of my equities
claims.claim: Rob discretionarily sold equities in the April 2025 tariff tantrum and lost relative performance; systematic Rob did better.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: which is what you would have expected if this genuinely was a like a a novel and interesting piece of information
claims.claim: The bond market reaction to the new Fed chair nomination was muted (no 50bp two-year move), so it was probably not the genuine cause of the silver crash.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: No one really knows what's going to happen, uh, in May.
claims.claim: Whether the new Fed chair will cut rates for the president or act independently is unknowable, though he is seen as relatively sane and possibly hawkish.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: I think it had much more to do with positioning and how people had been piling into this
claims.claim: The silver sell-off was driven by crowded positioning, including Chinese retail, rather than the Fed chair news.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: being a systematic diversified investor, I think is so much better than trying to make any sense of this from a discretionary point of view
claims.claim: Systematic diversification beats discretionary attempts to interpret political and market events.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: Google said that it's planning to double its CapEx this year to as much as $185 billion to really bet huge on AI.
claims.claim: Alphabet doubling AI capex to $185 billion suggests a possible bubble.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: there's a lot of breath because the percentage or 64 means that there are 64 of the market that in the portfolio it tracks that are quote-unquote trending
claims.claim: A trend barometer of 64 means 64% of tracked markets trend, indicating broad trend breadth that is supportive for CTAs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: the financial sectors like equities, a bit of currency, some of the fixed income markets even are supporting the um um P&L this month
claims.claim: February 2026 trend profits came from equities, currencies, fixed income, natural gas, meats and grains, a broad base.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um most CTAs who trade it would probably be short.
claims.claim: Most CTAs trading Bitcoin futures were likely short after the sell-off.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: Beta 50 up 33 basis points, up 5.38% so far this year, so very strong.
claims.claim: Early Feb 2026: BTOP50 +5.38% YTD, SG CTA +5%, SG Trend +5.25%, short-term traders +2.37%, MSCI World +1.76%, S&P 500 +0.63% YTD.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG indices, MSCI World, S&P 500

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: if you're targeting say a 15% risk target on each of them, you'll end up with a 15% risk target on the entire book cuz it's perfectly correlated.
claims.claim: With vol-targeted instruments, portfolio risk depends only on correlations; diversification means you must scale up positions to hit the book risk target.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: I get numbers of between four and five.
claims.claim: Compensating for diversification across instruments requires multiplying positions by about four to five; without it a 15% target gives about 3%.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: 0.7 is actually um roughly speaking the ratio between the correlation between the underlying instrument returns and the correlation between what happens if you trend follow those those instruments
claims.claim: The 0.7 figure in Rob's book is the ratio of trend-strategy correlation to underlying return correlation, not a fixed book correlation.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: you can use you can get can just use a rolling estimation window of about 6 months works quite well
claims.claim: Estimate book correlation from the combined P&L streams over a rolling 6-month window, optionally exponentially weighted; this includes asset and signal correlation.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: it's better to estimate them separately and then combine them together if that's what you want to do.
claims.claim: Volatility and correlation have different predictability, so estimate them separately and combine them into the covariance matrix.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: if you do a regression of next month's volatility on last month's volatility, you get an R squared of about 0.35.
claims.claim: Volatility is predictable (R-squared about 0.35 month-on-month), correlation less so (0.2-0.25), and means are unpredictable noise.
claims.indicator: predictability R-squared of vol, correlation, mean

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: you probably only use something like about a 6-month rolling estimate versus about a 1-month rolling estimate for vol
claims.claim: Use about a 6-month window for correlation and about 1 month for volatility, since correlation structure changes more slowly.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: the nice thing about doing things in a vol targeted way is you you don't need to estimate vols again.
claims.claim: When instruments are already vol-targeted, portfolio construction only needs correlations.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: we're going to divide um our market universe into three categories: traditional markets, alternative markets, and alternative esoteric markets.
claims.claim: The Man AHL paper classifies trend markets by liquidity and complexity into traditional, alternative and esoteric (China futures, physical crypto) and studies where returns come from.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: following portfolio is actually coming from my kind of risk on risk off factor, which I'm trend following.
claims.claim: A large part of trend returns is a risk-on/risk-off factor (as in 2008: bonds up, equities down), and the remainder is idiosyncratic.
claims.indicator: PCA first principal component of trend returns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: 45% idiosyncratic, 55% factors
claims.claim: Traditional CTA returns are about 55% factor and 45% idiosyncratic.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: in these unusual markets, these these alternative and these esoteric markets, it's more like 1/3 2/3
claims.claim: Alternative and esoteric markets are about one third factor and two thirds idiosyncratic, so they add weird, diversifying sources of return.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: only about 30% of their portfolio needs to should be going into these traditional markets
claims.claim: An unconstrained Sharpe-maximising optimisation puts about 30% in traditional markets and 70% in alternatives (about 5% in crypto), although large CTAs cannot do this because of capacity.
claims.conditions: liquidity and capacity constraints ignored

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: let's focus in on periods when equity markets fell.
claims.claim: Optimising for periods when equities fell gives a different answer than the generic optimisation, because investors buy trend for tail protection.
claims.conditions: for investors using CTAs as crisis alpha

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: You want to have 50% traditional markets
claims.claim: For crisis protection the optimal portfolio is about 50% traditional markets because their high factor share (short equities, long bonds) pays in crises.
claims.indicator: traditional market weight in crisis-conditional portfolio
claims.direction: long trend in traditional futures for crisis alpha
claims.conditions: when diversifying a 60/40 portfolio

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: because in a crisis um you basically want to just make fairly big bets on going 2008, going short equities, long bonds.
claims.claim: In a crisis a CTA needs large bets on short equities and long bonds, not exotic markets.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um, because a lot of these things in a crisis you do want to go short, because a lot of them trade like risk-on assets.
claims.claim: Many alternative markets trade like risk-on assets, and may be hard to short or illiquid in a crisis.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: Um, I'm only using 30% of my cash as margin. So, you know, a typical CTA, that number's 20%, and that's super cash efficient.
claims.claim: Futures trading uses only about 20-30% of cash as margin, making CTAs cash efficient; alternative markets need more margin.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: So, we end up with 70% in traditional markets and just just 30% in the the old the alternative markets.
claims.claim: Adding cash efficiency as a constraint shifts the optimum to about 70% traditional futures and 30% alternatives.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: So, you know, in 2008, the fact that CTAs had plenty of cash, daily liquidity, no gating meant that many people used them as cash machines
claims.claim: Cash efficiency matters most when cash is needed: in 2008 investors drew on CTAs as a source of ready cash.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: you would go for a portfolio that probably trades more markets
claims.claim: To maximise standalone long-term Sharpe, trade more (including alternative) markets; to get equity-crisis protection, choose managers focused on traditional liquid futures.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: what's the best manager fit for me in terms of what my objective is with investing with the CTA
claims.claim: Manager selection depends on investor objective: choose a traditional-futures manager for tail protection and cash needs.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: all the systematic finance is machine learning
claims.claim: Systematic finance has always used supervised machine learning in the form of regression and optimisation, blending into unsupervised and neural-network methods.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: their sort of thesis is that that basically these people are becoming more and more like each other
claims.claim: FT Alphaville thesis: finance quants and AI labs converge in workflow, hiring and technology stack.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: I think the people who are doing it best are ones who are using it in very tightly defined areas.
claims.claim: AI works best in tightly defined areas such as execution research, where tick data is rich and fits non-linear models; much of fund AI is marketing or blue-sky.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author, ex-AHL/AQR)
claims.quote: many of the top AI researchers are making far more money than than any person quant in finance is
claims.claim: AI researchers now get non-competes, gardening leave and nine-figure offers, exceeding quant pay.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: some CTAs will take basically binary positions, so they'll you know, they'll they'll kind of go from fully short to fully long
claims.claim: CTAs differ in how position size follows the trend signal: some take binary full-long or full-short positions, while others scale continuously with forecast strength; binary systems get much less benefit from forecast scaling when a trend ends abruptly.
claims.conditions: Design choice that decides exposure in a parabolic move.
claims.testable: yes - binary versus continuous forecast scaling can be backtested

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I have a daily rebalance, so I didn't do any trading in silver during Friday itself cuz my position was based on Thursday's close
claims.claim: A daily-rebalanced system sizes positions from the prior close, so on a gap day such as 30 Jan 2026 it cannot reduce exposure intraday; the loss is limited only because volatility-scaling had already cut the position in the days before.
claims.indicator: daily rebalance using previous close, silver
claims.direction: position cut ahead of the crash by earlier volatility rises
claims.conditions: Gap risk remains for any end-of-day system; only earlier vol-scaling protects it.
claims.testable: yes - execution lag and gap losses are measurable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I guess you could have also been stopped out on freaky Friday because the move was so big
claims.claim: A trader using a hard stop based on the recent high (possibly vol-linked) could have been stopped out on the crash day itself, so whether a stop-loss rule helps in a parabolic reversal depends on its exact definition.
claims.indicator: stop-loss defined from the recent high
claims.direction: stop triggers on a large one-day fall
claims.conditions: Depends on the stop rule and its volatility multiple.
claims.testable: partly - stop rules can be backtested for gap days

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: a 25% fall probably still would have breached any reasonable stop
claims.claim: Even a volatility-widened stop would probably have been breached by a 25% one-day fall, so stops do not remove gap risk; the size of the position, not the stop, determines the loss.
claims.conditions: Gap moves bypass stops, so sizing is the main protection.
claims.testable: yes - gap size versus stop distance is measurable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe become a little bit complacent thinking that these are all the same to trade
claims.claim: After a long rally in precious metals, traders can become complacent and assume silver and platinum are as liquid as gold, but they are different markets with different liquidity and crash risk.
claims.indicator: silver and platinum versus gold liquidity
claims.direction: liquidity risk underestimated in the less liquid metals
claims.conditions: Applies to crowded, extended rallies.
claims.testable: partly - liquidity differences across metals can be measured

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I might kind of have a fairly broad liquidity filter
claims.claim: A small account can use a broader liquidity filter than large CTAs and so holds instruments that big CTAs avoid or hold small, which gives it extra markets but also more exposure to thin-market liquidity gaps.
claims.indicator: liquidity filter relative to account size
claims.conditions: Small accounts only; capacity limits large CTAs.
claims.testable: yes - liquidity filter thresholds can be set from volume and open interest

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if confirmed, we will have a new Fed chair with the name of Kevin Walsh
claims.claim: Kevin Warsh was named as the nominee for Fed chair around the time of the 30 January 2026 silver crash, a surprise relative to expectations, and was taken by many as the proximate cause of the precious-metals sell-off.
claims.direction: tighter policy narrative for precious metals
claims.conditions: Time-bound event; the speakers doubt it was the real cause.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: he does he does have some opinions that are less mainstream around things like QE and the Fed balance sheet
claims.claim: The Fed chair nominee holds less mainstream views on QE and the Fed balance sheet but is seen as conventional or even hawkish on interest-rate setting, so the policy mix could differ from what the president wants.
claims.indicator: Fed balance sheet and QE policy
claims.direction: policy uncertainty rather than clear direction
claims.conditions: Depends on confirmation and how the board votes.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Trump always chickens out of the taco trade
claims.claim: Markets have largely shrugged off the president's policy shocks since early 2025, partly because of a 'TACO' pattern (he backs down) and because many do not take threats seriously, so Rob's initial expectation of a bad market was wrong.
claims.indicator: equity reaction to tariff and policy announcements
claims.conditions: Observed over the first year; may not hold if a shock is not reversed.
claims.testable: partly - post-announcement returns can be studied

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: let's not forget it was Trump who appointed Powell
claims.claim: A president's appointment says little about a Fed chair's later independence: Powell was appointed by Trump and then resisted pressure, and once in office chairs cannot be removed and care about their legacy.
claims.direction: appointee may act against the appointer's wishes
claims.conditions: Depends on legal protection of the Fed from removal.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's not like he can decide what interest rates are going to do
claims.claim: The Fed chair is one of 12 FOMC votes and cannot set rates alone; the real independence risk is a pending Supreme Court ruling that may let the president remove governors and pack the board.
claims.indicator: FOMC voting structure, Supreme Court ruling on Fed removal
claims.direction: independence risk if the ruling favours the president
claims.conditions: Time-bound legal decision.
claims.testable: no - depends on a court ruling

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: my risk is a little bit higher than it has been for a while, so that kind of matches up with your trend barometer
claims.claim: A system that scales positions with forecast strength runs higher realised risk when many markets trend strongly, so portfolio risk rises with trend breadth (the barometer).
claims.direction: risk rises when breadth of trends is high
claims.conditions: Applies to continuous forecast-scaled systems.
claims.testable: yes - realised vol versus trend breadth can be tested

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: as long as your correlation estimate's quite slow, like 6 months is pretty good, then that's going to be al- effectively irrelevant
claims.claim: Extra trading caused by updating a slow (six-month) correlation estimate is negligible compared with the trading caused by signals, so a time-varying estimate has little cost compared with a fixed assumption.
claims.conditions: Slow estimation window of about six months.
claims.testable: yes - turnover from estimate changes can be measured

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: this is a paper about not really about better models or faster signals
claims.claim: The Man AHL paper argues that differences between trend managers come mainly from which markets they trade (the market universe), not from better models or faster signals.
claims.conditions: Paper's central thesis; evidence in factor and idiosyncratic decomposition.
claims.testable: yes - testable by comparing universe versus speed contributions

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: that kind of first principal component didn't contribute much
claims.claim: January 2026 trend profits did not come from the risk-on/risk-off factor (bonds flat, equities slightly up) but from idiosyncratic sources such as gold, silver and natural gas, an example of returns from alternative-style markets.
claims.indicator: first principal component of trend returns, January 2026
claims.direction: idiosyncratic metals and gas drove returns
claims.conditions: Month-specific example.
claims.testable: yes - PCA decomposition can be repeated on the index
